author.name: Michel de Montaigne
author.biography: Montaigne left his work as a magistrate to write at his estate, but public life did not leave him alone: he later served as mayor of Bordeaux. Friendship, illness and religious war kept testing the distance between a principle and a lived experience. In the Essays, he makes that testing personal. His own habits, fears and changes of mind become material for asking what any human being can confidently claim to know.

hook.text: How well do you know the person you have been all your life?

paragraphs: Montaigne begins with a subject always available and never entirely understood: himself. His habits, illnesses, friendships, fears and changes of mind become material for thought.

The essays wander because their author is testing what he thinks rather than always presenting a conclusion already secured. An anecdote from antiquity can meet a bodily discomfort or an admission of ignorance. The movement gives philosophical inquiry the texture of an actual person discovering the limits of his own account.

That intimacy does not make the book merely private. Montaigne keeps returning to education, cruelty, custom and the ease with which people call unfamiliar practices barbarous. Knowing oneself can become a way of losing confidence in one's right to judge everybody else.
Read a single essay without insisting that every turn serve a straight line. What could you learn if changing your mind ceased to feel like evidence that you had failed?

orientation.text: The essays vary greatly in length and were revised over time. You can enter through an individual topic while remaining attentive to changes within the essay itself.
